title: Transient demand hopper — HC rotation & pricing sensitivity simulation
summary: A simulation-driven playbook that models short, high-intensity demand spikes ("hopper" events) and evaluates a rotational headcount pool + pricing levers to preserve margin and SLA. Includes per-scenario P&L and recommended operational triggers.
content:
Context and problem statement:
We frequently see transient, high-intensity traffic bursts from a small number of customers or new feature launches. These "hopper" events last 1–14 days and can double token throughput for specific routes. Current fixed-capacity hiring and reserve-burst commitments either leave us overprovisioned during steady-state or force expensive on-demand GPU usage during spikes.

Objective:
- Build a lightweight simulation that couples: baseline demand, hopper event probability and size distribution, rotational headcount ("flex-squad") activation, and three pricing response levers.
- Output: monthly P&L delta, token-level marginal cost, SLA risk (p95 latency breach probability), and recommended trigger rules.

Key assumptions (configurable):
- Baseline throughput: 30B tokens/mo (company-wide hosted API routes subset).
- Hopper frequency: 3 events per quarter (Poisson lambda tuned from historical samples).
- Hopper intensity: median x1.8, 90th pct x3.5, duration median 4 days.
- Flex-squad pool: 18 FTE-equivalents (rotation schedule provides 6 FTEs on-call per week). Average loaded cost per FTE (fully burdened): $15,500/mo.
- Reserved capacity cushion: 20% baseline (dedicated) at committed cost.
- On-demand GPU marginal cost (if no flex-squad): $0.035 per 1k tokens (model mix weighted).
- Quantization and batching savings achievable when flex-squad activates: 12% token-cost reduction vs on-demand baseline.
- Pricing levers: immediate temporary surcharge (+15%), dynamic tiered discounting (volume buckets), and priority queuing (latency-risk tradeoff).

Scenarios modeled:
1) Baseline + no hopper (control).
2) Hopper events with no flex-squad — rely on on-demand GPUs.
3) Hopper events with flex-squad + conservative pricing surcharge as deterrent.
4) Hopper events with flex-squad + aggressive priority pricing + route-level throttles.

Selected outputs (example month snapshots):
- Scenario 2 (no flex-squad) example month with a single x3 spike for 5 days:
  - Extra tokens from hopper: +0.5B tokens month
  - On-demand GPU cost: 0.5B / 1k * $0.035 = $17,500 (model-weighted) -> plus kernel licensing/ops adders => ~$27k
  - SLA risk (p95 latency breach): 22% observed in sim runs
  - Net margin delta: -6.8% vs baseline

- Scenario 3 (flex-squad + surcharge):
  - Activation cost (pro-rated rotas): additional payroll layering = +$8,700 for the month (rotational coverage proration)
  - Quantization & batching savings during activation: -$3,000 vs on-demand usage for same token volume
  - Customer churn/rate reduction due to surcharge: simulated elasticity 0.06 (small drop in usage) -> revenue net effect neutral to +1% depending on elasticity curve
  - SLA risk: 6%
  - Net margin delta: -1.9% vs baseline (acceptable)

Sensitivity analysis highlights:
- Hopper size sensitivity: beyond x2.4 intensity, on-demand costs escalate superlinearly (because host-level batching breaks and more requests fall back to high-cost execution paths). At x3+, margin erosion >10% without flex-squad.
- Hopper frequency sensitivity: if lambda >6/quarter, hiring 6 additional steady-state FTEs becomes cheaper than relying on either on-demand or a larger flex pool (breakeven boundary in sheet).
- Pricing elasticity: temporary +15% surcharge protects margin only if customer price elasticity <0.12 for high-volume enterprise routes. For mid-market routes elasticity is closer to 0.25 => surcharge harms net revenue.

Operational playbook (recommended triggers):
- Soft trigger: single route token rate > 2.5x baseline sustained 12+ hours -> auto-flag and notify flex-squad lead.
- Hard trigger: single route token rate > 3.5x baseline sustained 6+ hours OR system-wide token utilization > 85% -> activate flex-squad, enable temporary +10–15% surcharge on affected route, and open priority queuing.
- Escalation: if p95 latency > target after 2 hours of flex-squad activation, shift traffic to compatible quantized model variant (auto-fallback) and recommend sales outreach for affected customers.

Financial checklist to execute before go-live:
- Create a dedicated flex-squad cost center and tagging for route-level P&L attribution (Jira FIN-7342).
- Add one-time tooling budget for routing automations (estimated $32k).
- Define terms for temporary surcharge (legal + CS review) and UI messaging template.

Next steps / experiments to run (links in linked_artifacts):
- Run 10k Monte Carlo sims with alternate elasticity priors (sheet tab: sims-10k).
- Pilot flex-squad rotation on two mid-market clusters for 30 days and capture real activation costs + customer reaction.
- Add more realistic model-mix displacement curves to the simulator (PR #212 in capacity-sim repo).

Open questions / risks:
- Behavioral: will enterprise customers accept surcharges on short activations? Need controlled playbook + account manager alignment.
- Technical: are all candidate routes compatible with quantized fallback without accuracy regressions? Rapid evals required.
- Accounting: how do we treat flex-squad overtime and contractor swaps vs FTE costs for long-running seasons?

Appendix (quick numbers extract):
- Flex-squad pool sizing sensitivity (breakeven approximate):
  - 6 FTEs on-call: breakeven if hopper frequency <= 2.5 / quarter and median intensity <= x2.0
  - 12 FTEs on-call: breakeven if hopper frequency 3–5 / quarter and median intensity <= x2.6
  - Hire 6 perm FTEs if expected sustained lambda >6/quarter (cost +$930k annual fully loaded)

- Pricing point break-evens (back-of-envelope):
  - Temporary +10% surcharge: protects margin up to x2.5 intensity for enterprise routes (elasticity <0.1).
  - Temporary +20% surcharge: risk of >10% churn on mid-market routes.

- Quick action item list (owners):
  - Ethan Li: wire up Monte Carlo runs + add route-level latency outputs (due 2026-12-09)
